learn.title: Comparisons with (not) as ... as: adjectives and adverbs
learn.html:
Use as + adjective/adverb + as to say that two things are equal, and not as ... as to say that one is less than the other.

StructureExampleMeaning
as + adjective + asThe pants are just as comfortable as my jeans.They are equally comfortable.
not as + adjective + asThe pants are not as comfortable as my jeans.The pants are less comfortable.
as + adverb + asI tried as hard as I could.I made my maximum effort.
not as + adverb + asHe doesn't run as fast as his brother.He runs more slowly.
  • To add emphasis: just as, exactly as. To soften or firmly deny: not quite as, not nearly as.
  • After the second as you can use a pronoun (as me) or a pronoun with a verb (as I do).
  • You can avoid the comparative: A isn't as big as B means the same as B is bigger than A.

watch.wrong: This sweater is not so warm than that one.
watch.right: This sweater is not as warm as that one.
watch.why: The structure is as ... as; never use than with this pattern.

watch.wrong: My jeans are not as new that yours.
watch.right: My jeans are not as new as yours.
watch.why: The second term of the comparison takes as.

watch.wrong: He sings as good as his brother.
watch.right: He sings as well as his brother.
watch.why: With a verb we use the adverb (well), not the adjective (good).

watch.wrong: She is as tall like her mother.
watch.right: She is as tall as her mother.
watch.why: Don't use like in this structure: as ... as.

learn.title: as + much / many / little / few + noun + as
learn.html:
To compare quantities with a noun, use as + determiner + noun + as. The choice depends on whether the noun is countable or uncountable.

TypeStructureExample
Countable (plural)as many / as few + noun + asShe doesn't wear as many bright colors as she should.
Uncountableas much / as little + noun + asShe spends as little time as possible on her makeup.
Verb + quantityverb + as much asI don't like short hair as much as long hair.
Maximumas ... as possible / as ... as you canTake as much time as you need.

In Spanish we use tanto/a/os/as ... como, which changes with gender and number. In English only one thing matters: whether the noun is countable (many) or uncountable (much).

watch.wrong: I don't have as much shoes as my sister.
watch.right: I don't have as many shoes as my sister.

watch.wrong: She spends as many time as possible at the mirror.
watch.right: She spends as much time as possible at the mirror.

watch.wrong: I don't spend as much money than you.
watch.right: I don't spend as much money as you.
watch.why: It closes with as, not with than.

watch.wrong: There are not as much stores here as downtown.
watch.right: There are not as many stores here as downtown.

learn.title: Negative questions
learn.html:
Negative questions start with a negative auxiliary verb: Isn't ...? Don't you ...? Doesn't she ...? In English they are not used to ask for neutral information: they express an attitude.

UseExampleWhat you mean
Giving an opinionIsn't this jacket great? / Don't you think it's great?I think it's great and I hope you agree.
Suggesting an ideaIt'd look good, don't you think?I propose something and I want your agreement.
Showing surpriseIsn't it on sale? / Doesn't she like it?I expected a yes, and I'm surprised it's not.
  • Form: negative auxiliary + subject + verb. With be: Aren't they expensive? With the simple present: Don't you like it?
  • The answer is based on reality, not on the question: Isn't it nice? — Yes, it is. / No, it isn't.
  • Don't you think ...? at the end of a sentence softens an opinion.

watch.wrong: Don't it look good on me?
watch.right: Doesn't it look good on me?
watch.why: With it we use doesn't, not don't.

watch.wrong: Doesn't he likes the blue shirt?
watch.right: Doesn't he like the blue shirt?
watch.why: After doesn't, the verb goes in its base form.
With a regular verb we use the auxiliary do/does, not be.
Think is a regular verb: Don't you think ...?

learn.title: Punctuation in writing: commas, dashes and exclamation marks
learn.html:
Good punctuation makes a text about fashion, tips or recommendations read naturally.

MarkUseExample
Comma (,)Separates a list of three or more itemsGet rid of stained, torn, or out-of-style clothing.
No commaNot used in a list of only two itemsGet rid of torn or out-of-style clothing.
Dash (–)Adds or explains something moreSilk may feel nice, but be careful – shiny fabrics can make you look heavier.
Exclamation mark (!)Adds emphasisDeveloping your own style is not as hard as you might think!
  • The comma before the last and (serial comma) is optional in English; be consistent throughout the text.
  • Don't overuse exclamation marks: one per paragraph is usually enough.

watch.wrong: I bought a shirt a skirt a belt and a scarf.
watch.right: I bought a shirt, a skirt, a belt, and a scarf.
watch.why: In a list of three or more items, separate them with commas.
With only two items, no comma is used.

watch.wrong: Be careful, shiny fabrics can make you look heavier.
watch.right: Be careful – shiny fabrics can make you look heavier.
watch.why: The dash introduces an explanation; a single comma would join the two ideas badly.

learn.title: Functions: summarizing, following up and giving opinions
learn.html:
• She seems to have a lot of different interests. — summarize what someone said, to show you are following the conversation.
  • So she's a real book lover. — summarize in your own words.
  • Now, doesn't she travel a lot? — use Now to introduce a follow-up question and shift to another aspect of the topic.
  • Overall, I think ... — give a general opinion at the end.
  • Isn't it great? / Don't you think so? — ask for agreement.
  • It's just right. / It's not quite my style. — give an opinion about a garment.
  • Do you have it in a bigger size? — ask for a different size.
  • I'm just looking around, thanks. — respond to the salesperson.

write.model:
How to develop your own style

Developing your own style is not as hard as you might think! You do not need a lot of money or a famous designer. You only need to know yourself and to be brave.

First, look at your wardrobe. Choose the clothes you love and think about why you love them. Your favorite jeans may be as comfortable as pajamas, and a simple cotton shirt can look as elegant as a silk blouse. Pay attention to materials, colors and patterns: cotton, leather and wool each give a different feeling, and red, black and blue are easy to combine.

Second, do not be afraid to experiment. Wear a bright scarf with a plain jacket, or try boots with a long skirt. You do not need as many clothes as you think. In fact, a small wardrobe with as few items as ten or fifteen pieces can be just as useful as a huge one. Quality is as important as quantity.

Third, copy ideas, but never copy people. Look at magazines, shop windows and friends — and then make the look yours! Your style should be as personal as your handwriting.

Finally, be patient. It takes time to find your style, but the more you try, the easier it gets. Have fun, and remember: the best outfit is the one that makes you feel as confident as you really are.

write.model:
Hi Nuria,

Thanks for asking me about a gift for your sister's birthday. I think I can help! She seems to have a lot of interests: she seems to love reading, and she seems to be interested in cooking, too. She doesn't like fancy jewelry, does she? And isn't she always carrying a tote bag with her?

I have two ideas. The first one is a cookbook with recipes from different regions of Mexico. It is as beautiful as an art book, and it is not as expensive as a kitchen gadget. The second option is a leather bag. It is as practical as a backpack, but it is not as cheap as a book. Isn't it better to give something she will use every day? Doesn't she say that she needs a new bag?

Now, one question: what is your budget? If you want to spend as little as possible, the book is the better choice. If you can spend more, the bag will last for ten years, and it is as stylish as many designer bags.

Overall, I think the cookbook is the best option, because it is as personal as a handwritten letter, and you can add a note inside. Let me know what you decide!

Best wishes,
Paola

reading.title: A Makeover for Renata
reading.intro: Read the text about an afternoon of shopping and answer the questions.
paragraphs: Last spring my friend Renata asked me to give her a makeover. She is a talented architect, but she never cared about her appearance. She wore the same baggy gray sweater almost every day, and her jeans were scruffy and out of shape. "I don't have as much time as other people," she told me, "and shopping isn't as fun as it looks." I didn't agree, but I decided to help her anyway.

We started on Saturday morning at a big department store that has a huge selection of clothes. Renata tried on a long-sleeved navy blue turtleneck, a pair of dark denim jeans, and a wool coat. At first she was choosy about everything. "Isn't this coat a little expensive?" she asked. "It is," I said, "but it's as warm as two sweaters, and it will last for years. Don't you think that's worth it?" She laughed and finally agreed to buy it, because it was on the sale rack, so she didn't have to pay full price.

The biggest surprise was color. Renata thought she looked best in gray and black, but I put a deep blue scarf around her neck, and she was thrilled. "Doesn't it look great?" the saleswoman said. It really did. We also learned that bright colors were not as hard to wear as she imagined. A solid color shirt with a floral-print scarf worked beautifully, and she didn't spend as much money as she feared.

Here are the three rules we learned. First, try everything on before you decide, because sizes are never the same in every store. Second, look around before you buy: the first shop is not always the best one. Third, choose clothes that fit your daily life. A beautiful silk blouse isn't practical if you ride a bike to work every day.

By the afternoon we were tired, but happy. We had lunch, and Renata said, "I always thought fashion was only about looks, but now I think comfort matters just as much." I agreed. A good outfit isn't only about being stylish; it's also about feeling like yourself. She still wears sneakers to work, but now she chooses a fitted jacket and a nice belt, and her colleagues keep telling her how different she looks.

Last week she called me. "Overall, I think shopping isn't as boring as I used to believe," she said. "Now, aren't you free this Saturday? I want to look for a leather bag." Of course I'm free. After all, a good makeover isn't about changing who you are. It's about spending a little time and a little money on yourself, so that you can walk out of the house feeling just a bit more confident.
